greek.title: The Athletic Crown and Civic Glory
greek.body:
When Diagoras of Rhodes won the boxing crown at Olympia in 464 BCE, his victory was more than personal triumph. His sons would later win there too, carrying him on their shoulders through the cheering crowd. A spectator called out that Diagoras should die now, having reached the peak of mortal happiness.

This fusion of physical prowess and moral worth defined Greek ἀρετή. Homer's warriors proved their excellence in battle; later citizens displayed it in athletic contests, philosophical debate, or civic service. The gymnasium trained both body and character. Pindar's victory odes celebrated athletes as embodiments of divine favor and hereditary virtue, their crowns of wild olive bringing honor to their entire city.

Excellence demanded witnesses. Private virtue meant nothing; ἀρετή required public demonstration and communal recognition.
